title: No 10 appears to backtrack on PM's freedom of movement referendum suggestion
description: Downing Street has appeared to backtrack on the prime minister's suggestion that he could call another referendum on whether to join the EU's freedom
body: Downing Street has appeared to backtrack on the prime minister's suggestion that he could call another referendum on whether to join the EU's freedom of movement.Asked earlier by broadcasters if he could introduce freedom of movement without a referendum, Andy Burnham said "no".But sources told the BBC no decision on that has been made and the prime minister's deputy spokesperson later said the government was not going to "get ahead" of how to consult the public.Burnham has ruled out major changes to the UK's relationship with the EU before the next general election but says he wants start a conversation about potential options.He told broadcasters that he would "never move ahead of the British public when it comes to Brexit".Migration dominated debate during the 2016 Brexit campaign, with the Leave campaign raising issues about freedom of movement allowing any EU citizen to move to the UK.Burnham has said he is committed to Labour's 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.And he has previously stressed any changes would require a mandate at a general election, which is due by 2029.After lengthy questioning about the issue, Number 10 sought to clarify the prime minister's remarks, saying: "The prime minister isn't proposing a return to freedom of movement or any option.""He is crucially not leaning either way and that will be for the British public to decide," the prime minister's deputy spokeswoman said."What he wants to do first is have a conversation with the public. The process will follow."She added: "The PM thinks the Brexit deal is not good enough."Freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to travel, live, study and work in any member country, is a precondition of membership of the EU's single market.The single market enables goods, services and people to move freely between member states, with countries also applying many common rules and standards.In an interview with the Sunday Times, external, Burnham said he would welcome an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and the EU.The PM argued that the type of migration had changed since Brexit, with more foreigners moving permanently.In contrast, he suggested that when the UK was a member of the EU, migration was "generally younger people", who would spend a few years in the country before returning home.However, Burnham added: "I can't see myself ever recommending anything that would involve joining the euro or Schengen."The Schengen Agreement, which the UK was not part of when it was in the EU, allows passport-free travel across member countries. The UK was able to keep the pound when it was an EU member, but the bloc has pushed new members to adopt the Euro.Burnham has argued that since Brexit, the UK has lost immigration control the country previously had."For instance, the small boats crisis has arisen in the last 10 years because we lost that returns agreement when people came here that we could work with other countries to return them," he told broadcasters.The Conservatives and Reform UK both oppose a return to free movement with the EU.However, the Liberal Democrats have argued that allowing freedom of movement would help economic growth.Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch argued most people who voted for Brexit did so because they did not want free movement, while Reform leader Nigel Farage has said such a move would be "a total betrayal of Brexit Britain".Farage told broadcasters he was "up for the fight again" on the EU and an "election is coming" to decide that."Crucially, [Burnham] goes to Brussels on 20 November for a key summit - he must not sign up to anything there without at least putting those minor changes to a general election," he said.

schema.headline: No 10 appears to backtrack on PM's freedom of movement referendum suggestion

title: Anthropic's blockbuster share listing - 5 surprising things we now know
description: Image source, EPAImage caption, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has become a key figure in the current AI era.ByKali HaysTechnology reporterUpdated 3 hours
body: Image source, EPAImage caption, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has become a key figure in the current AI era.ByKali HaysTechnology reporterUpdated 3 hours agoArtificial intelligence (AI) firm Anthropic just released the required paperwork ahead of its long-anticipated debut on the US stock market.The 335-page document included fresh details of how the Claude chatbot owner makes money, what it spends that money on and who it is controlled by. Anthropic also detailed some of the the risks it claimed AI technology poses, including how it could take human lives. That information sat alongside the many purported benefits of the technology.Here are five key points worth highlighting from the filing.1. Armageddon is an occupational hazardEvery public company has to tell potential investors how things could go wrong.Anthropic's "risk factors" were unique, also disclosing how the AI technology it is developing could doom humanity as a whole."Sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," Anthropic said.It noted that less than a year ago, a hacking group Anthropic believed to be sponsored by China "manipulated" Claude to successfully intrude on a number of institutions, including large technology companies, financial institutions, chemical manufacturing companies and government agencies.But Anthropic said its success is dependent on its ability to constantly "develop, improve, and deploy the most advanced, capable, and useful AI models".One of the most significant risks to that ability is Anthropic's access to infrastructure it needs, including computer chips and data centres, to build, train and operate the models that underpin its technology. 2. The company is haemorrhaging cashAnthropic has yet to disclose a target share price for its stock listing. The company is widely expected to debut with a market valuation of $2 trillion or more, making it the largest stock listing in history. But the figure will be heavily influenced by its financial performance. Anthropic lost $80.7bn (£60bn) in the first half of this year, double what it lost across 2025 altogether.The company's overall revenue was $16.2bn billion for the six-month period. Revenues are rising rapidly, but the firm has a long way to go before it breaks even. Troy Hooper, co-head of equity capital markets at Mergermarket, said Anthropic's revenue growth is "exceptional". But investors are "less forgiving" of tech companies promising huge future returns than they were even months ago, he added.Anthropic's debt picture is also unclear given it has a huge amount of accounting charges related to certain forms of investment."As a result, investors do not yet have a clear view of Anthropic's underlying profitability or whether its rate of cash generation is sufficient to support the business as it scales," Hooper added.3. But luckily it has plenty of cash on handDespite losing money, Anthropic has heaps of cash lying about. At $131.6bn, almost all of its cash in hand is defined as "working capital", meaning it can use the money to fund its operations day-to-day.Currently, Anthropic has more cash on hand than Meta and Google combined.Anthropic's costs could rise as it faces fierce competition for top staff and computing power from other AI giants. The leasing of data centres alone is costing the company $321.4bn so far this year.Hooper said such large costs are expected to grow. Even with this kind of cash, it won't be enough to maintain its business growth.Any investors in Anthropic "will be paying for future dominance, not present-day economics", he said.4. Anthropic relies on a few big customersAnthropic sees boundless ways it can sell its technology to customers.A large portion of its current business comes from just 250 major enterprise customers, which it says have paid it at least $10mn in the past year.An even smaller number, just five enterprise customers, make up a quarter of its current business.Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of Founder ETF, pointed out that "many top Anthropic customers have no long-term contract".The company's level of business concentration leaves Anthropic dependent on a small fraction of its paying customers to support its growth, with no guarantee it will continue. Anthropic also has enterprise relationships with the likes of Google and Amazon, both of which are also investors in the company "and competitors", creating potential business conflicts in the future, Monaghan noted. Anthropic said its overall enterprise customer base has grown rapidly, going from roughly 1,500 customers last year to almost 12,000 this year.Part of its growth strategy is offering Claude tools for free before working to "convert these users into paying customers over time".The strategy has led to Claude seeing "the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history", the company claimed.5. AI promises 'extraordinary' benefits to the worldFor all of the risks Anthropic has said AI poses, it also reiterated its claim AI will produce an "extraordinary" amount of good."Achieving our mission means the world gains the enormous benefits of frontier AI while mitigating the most significant risks," the company said.That mission is defined as: "The responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity.""We do not pursue projects based on commercial opportunity or research novelty alone; our efforts must advance our mission. "Such hypothetical benefits include progress in healthcare, like the development of bespoke treatments for illnesses and improved disease detection, tailored education and legal advice and making more efficient power grids and batteries.  Decades of scientific progress could be condensed into years, accelerating drug discovery, disease detection, and the delivery of personalized therapy. Anthropic said AI could provide individually tailored education and expert financial and legal advice, advance power grids and battery design for greater efficiency and reliability and help the "developing world" build more technological capabilities."Ultimately, we believe frontier AI will help drive global economic growth," the company said.

schema.headline: Anthropic's blockbuster share listing - 5 surprising things we now know

title: Star Trek actor Walter Koenig, who played Pavel Chekov, dies aged 90
description: Walter Koenig, who played the spirited Russian crewman Pavel Chekov in the original Star Trek TV series, has died aged 90.The US actor was a mainstay
body: Walter Koenig, who played the spirited Russian crewman Pavel Chekov in the original Star Trek TV series, has died aged 90.The US actor was a mainstay on the show as the eager and earnest navigator of the Starship Enterprise, from season two in 1967 until it ended in 1969, later reprising his role in the six original cast movies from 1979 through to 1991.In the mid-late 1990s, Koenig portrayed a very different character, the ruthless Psi Corps telepath Alfred Bester, in another sci-fi space series, Babylon 5.His Star Trek co-star George Takei led the tributes, external on social media on Monday, writing: "Walter was more than Chekov. He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man, and a loyal friend."Representatives for Koenig said in a statement given to the BBC: "Today we mourn the passing of Walter Koenig, whose talent, warmth, and unforgettable performances left a lasting mark on generations of fans around the world."They confirmed he had died "of old age at home in North Hollywood" on Sunday night, "surrounded by his daughter and niece".Koenig's Chekov added heart and humour to the adventures of the crew, led by William Shatner as Captain James T. Kirk.Takei, who played Hikaru Sulu, added: "Rest well, my dear friend. Keep navigating a steady course."Born in Chicago and raised in Manhattan, Koenig was the son of Soviet Jewish immigrants whose family had lived in Lithuania.He studied at the famous Neighborhood Playhouse School of the Theatre in New York, alongside the likes of James Caan, Christopher Lloyd and Dabney Coleman.His big break came as the capable young Chekov, who would often joke that everything was invented in Russia. The character was introduced to appeal to younger audiences, with his Beatles/Monkees-style mop-top haircut.But Star Trek creator Gene Roddenberry's studio also publicised the role as a response to criticism in Pravda, the main newspaper of the Soviet Communist Party, about the lack of a Russian character. This was a claim Koenig later denied.The American show, which aired during the Cold War and Space Race between the US and Soviet Union, imagined a future in which nations worked together to explore the galaxy, and Chekov's Russian heritage fitted that ideal.Koenig once said that the character's purpose on the NBC show was to "set out the bones of the plot and let McCoy, Spock and Kirk fill it in", according to the Hollywood Reporter., externalHe was arguably more integral to the movies, being nominated by the Academy of Science Fiction, Fantasy & Horror for his work on The Wrath of Khan (1982) and The Voyage Home (1986).Koenig's seventh Star Trek film appearance was a brief one in Generations (1994) - mainly a next generation film - and he later voiced President Anton Chekov in the modern series Star Trek: Picard in 2023.He also wrote an episode of the original show's animated series spin-off, in 1973, titled The Infinite Vulcan.

schema.headline: Star Trek actor Walter Koenig, who played Pavel Chekov, dies aged 90

title: Independent review announced into murder of student Henry Nowak
description: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced an independent review into the murder of Henry Nowak.The 18-year-old student was fatally stabbed in South
body: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced an independent review into the murder of Henry Nowak.The 18-year-old student was fatally stabbed in Southampton in December by Vickrum Digwa, who falsely claimed he had been racially abused and had acted in self-defence. Digwa was jailed for life on 1 June, with a minimum term of 21 years.Following the teenager's murder, police bodycam footage of him being handcuffed as he lay dying led to intense scrutiny of the Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary and sparked wider debates around knife laws, race, policing and public trust. The review, which was welcomed by Nowak's family, will be led by former Justice Secretary Alex Chalk KC."We must get to truth of what happened before, during and after that awful night and we must do everything in our power to ensure that no family suffers the same fate," Mahmood told the House of Commons on Monday. Mahmood said the review will investigate what was known about Nowak's killer and if there were missed opportunities to intervene as well as the treatment of his family in the justice system and whether they received enough support.In a statement published on Monday, the Home Office said the review will be carried out in two parts.Phase one will cover the police, health services, local authorities educational institutions and faith organisations, including if any concerns were raised relating to weapon possession and violent behavior, the statement said. It will also look to determine if there were missed opportunities to prevent Nowak's murder. Phase two will follow after the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) has concluded its investigation into the actions of police officers who attended the scene. It will consider the actions of the IOPC and "if necessary" the police, the Home Office added. The IOPC launched its own investigation into the response on the night of Nowak's death after bodycam footage showed the 18-year-old was handcuffed and left dying on the floor despite informing officers of his injuries.The investigation was launched despite a sentencing judge ruling Nowak would not have survived his injuries, however quickly he received treatment.The Nowak family described the announcement as a "significant moment in our fight for justice.""We hope this review, alongside the ongoing investigations and inquest, will finally uncover the full truth and deliver the accountability and meaningful change we have fought so hard for," they added in a statement."Our experience of the criminal justice system has been deeply disappointing, and we are determined that no other family should have to endure what we have." Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch welcomed the decision to launch the review."There must be proper accountability for those who failed Henry and his family," she said.The review is due to report in five months. Nowak, from Chafford Hundred in Essex, was a first-year accountancy and finance student at the University of Southampton when he was murdered.On the night of Nowak's muder, it was Digwa's brother who called 999, claiming Vickrum had been attacked "racially".Bodycam footage released by Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary, with the permission of Nowak's family, showed officers speaking to Digwa and others while Nowak lay on the ground.Nowak could be heard repeatedly saying that he had been stabbed and could not breathe.Violent disorder broke out in Southampton in the days following the release of the footage.After Digwa's sentencing, Nowak's father Mark called for a "full, fearless and transparent" investigation into the police response.But he also urged people not to use his son's death to "create further division, hatred or tension".

schema.headline: Independent review announced into murder of student Henry Nowak

title: Will the public change its mind about Meghan?
description: Meghan, who recently moved back to the UK with Prince Harry and their children, has frequently been accused of cutting off those once close to her.Her
body: Meghan, who recently moved back to the UK with Prince Harry and their children, has frequently been accused of cutting off those once close to her.Her treatment of her father was seen as a prime example."She ditched her family, ditched her dad, ditched most of her old friends, split Harry from William," wrote one commentator in 2020."Get on a plane and go see the poor man before it's too late," she was told on social media about her father.All of that might need to be viewed in a different and more sympathetic light.By 2019, Meghan had received disturbing allegations about Thomas Markle, in a letter from her father's first wife, Roslyn Loveless.She says it is why she kept her distance and also why she didn't bring her children to him, including when she moved to the United States with her family. That letter was shared with Meghan by the police, at a time when she was classified as a working royal. It's not clear who else knew about the letter, including Palace officials, but it must have been a sensitive matter for her.And according to the Sussexes' spokesman, Meghan believed an investigation into the allegations was going ahead, presumably at a time when she was on official trips and having to put on a brave face.There was also criticism levelled at Meghan in December 2025 when her father was in hospital in the Philippines, undergoing the amputation of his leg. "I don't want to die estranged from Meghan. I want to meet my grandkids. It might be nice to meet her husband too," Markle told the Mail on Sunday at the time. There was a media storm about whether Meghan was going to reach out to her father, culminating in a letter being delivered from her to her father, which at the time was assumed to be well-wishes.But that whole episode now looks different with the benefit of hindsight. That letter was a much more fraught affair. It revealed that Meghan knew about the allegations against her father. We now understand that Meghan was telling him he would never see his grandchildren.Thomas Markle has strongly denied all the allegations against him, saying they are "sick lies" which are trying to destroy his reputation.His daughter Samantha Markle has also rejected the claims, saying the stories are "fake news" and "clickbait". "There will be no legal action against my dad with no evidence in so many flimsy stories and my dad never had access to any such content and was in the hospital most of the time that he was there," she wrote on X on Sunday.Samantha also challenges the credibility of the letter written by her mother, Roslyn Loveless, which was shared with Meghan in 2019 and contained details of allegations of sexual abuse against Thomas Markle. When you look through photos of Meghan at events over the last seven years, you wonder what was going on behind the familiar smile.Those years have seen Netflix films, a tell-all memoir by Prince Harry, cookery series, podcasts and TV interviews. But a hidden narrative has been running in the background.Meghan's supporters have pointed to other factors in how she has been treated, with racism and sexism part of that toxic mix.But maybe there was also a sense of not knowing the authentic person behind the polished Brand Meghan.On Instagram, she has curated her life to look idyllic, but perhaps she'll get a more generous hearing now that her back story is as messy and imperfect as everyone else's.It could still be an uphill struggle to become more popular, beyond her own vocal, core group of supporters.A survey from YouGov earlier this month found 22% of people had a positive view of Meghan, compared with 49% who dislike her.That suggests there is still some way to go before Meghan fully wins the trust of the public. Fascination, yes. But affection, not always.For the British public, Californian Meghan hasn't always translated well.But perhaps this complex, still developing story - and the light it sheds on previous years - might mean there's a more rounded view of her in the future.

schema.headline: Will the public change its mind about Meghan?

title: Serbia's student movement: How and why students brought down Vučić
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Although it was a students' movement that won Serbia's election, no student has been electedByPaul Ki
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Although it was a students' movement that won Serbia's election, no student has been electedByPaul KirbyEurope digital editorUpdated 8 hours agoTheirs is a movement born from tragedy that began with students blockading streets and turned into almost daily protests and a national movement against corruption and government negligence.In just under two years the students have succeeded in tearing up 14 years of political dominance under Aleksandar Vučić, who has seen support for his Serbian Progressive party (SNS) ebb away and ultimately fail in what became a referendum on the future of Serbia.From Belgrade to Novi Sad and Niš, the mood was euphoric as supporters gathered in town centres or in front of Student List headquarters. In a post on social media, the students declared "Serbia is free".Most symbolic of all was the demise of so-called Ćaciland, a pro-Vučić tent camp set up 18 months ago at Pioneers Park in central Belgrade in front of the Serbian parliament. Metal fences were torn down amid shouts of "Vučić is leaving".How the students changed SerbiaThey have no obvious leaders and have no grounding in politics, and yet the "Student List-Students Win" movement attracted anti-government voters across Serbian society.They fielded candidates for all 250 parliamentary seats, and yet no students were among them.As he joined the students marching towards Belgrade last week, lead candidate and cardiologist Ilija Srdanović said history was being rewritten: "The energy is unstoppable.""We offer our citizens the core values of civilised society, which this previous regime has taken away from our citizens for the last time," he told the BBC.It all began on 1 November 2024, when the concrete canopy collapsed outside Novi Sad train station, in Serbia's second biggest city, killing 16 people.The tragedy was seen as emblematic of widespread corruption. Critics linked the station's fatally flawed renovation to a president who had closely associated himself with the project."When the canopy collapsed that served as the last straw," says Helena Ivanov of the think tank the Henry Jackson Society. It was an emotional moment that triggered a spark and a national campaign of marches and events, she said, that captured the hearts and minds of Serbians in a way no opposition party had been able to do.From protests to direct challenge to VučićImage source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, Aleksandar Vučić conceded victory, but said the students' movement would failWhat started as weekly student protests demanding justice on university campuses and city streets soon became a national movement, often at a local level, that encompassed far more sections of Serbian society, including farmers, actors and judges.Vučić's SNS was clearly shaken and by January 2025 his prime minister had resigned "to defuse tensions". In March 2025 Belgrade saw Serbia's biggest ever anti-government protest and as the leaderless student movement increased in strength, they organised themselves through student assemblies or plenums.By the time Vučić had announced snap elections last month, they were ready. "They have been able to take that emotional momentum into a proper organisation and have people learn how to protect fairness at polling stations," Helena Ivanov explained."The message was clear: the rule of law and not ruled by the law," said Gordana Delić, head of the Balkans programme at the German Marshall Fund of the US, who said Sunday's vote was in effect a referendum.Initially Vučić sought to praise the protesters as "well-intentioned", but ahead of the elections he accused them of trying to "bring down" Serbia. Even after conceding victory on Sunday night he made the unfounded allegation that they had the support of unnamed "European countries and the American deep state".Who will run Serbia now?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Ilija Srdanović topped the Student List's candidates but is not seen as a likely prime ministerOne thing is clear, it will not be the students, as they were not standing for election. That was a calculated decision as the electorate would probably not have voted for a list of candidates with little life experience.Although their top candidate was Ilija Srdanović, a cardiology professor in Novi Sad, he is not really seen as a likely prime minister. Few candidates stand out as potential leaders.According to a final projection by independent polling groups CeSID and Ipsos, 141 people on the list have won seats in parliament. They include ex-basketball star Dejan Bodiroga (24th on the list), renowned actor Tihomir Stanić (8th), opera singer Nikola Mikić (46th), former National Bank of Serbia governor Dejan Šoškić (27th), and a rather large number of professors.Šoškić's name has been mentioned in connection with the top post. He has spoken out about reforms he would make to the economy, and he has been widely criticised in pro-government media.What is their programme?The elected MPs will have the task of fulfilling what is in effect a manifesto.In the words of the students themselves, they were looking for people who could enter institutions "do their jobs responsibly and not forget why they are there".Under an 11-point programme, , externalthe student movement wants to:Eradicate corruption by forming a police unit to arrest those responsible for itPurge officials in the internal affairs ministry of anyone who broke rules on cracking down on protesters, or anyone linked to organised crimeReform Serbia's skewed media scene and free the public broadcaster of political controlStop recruiting party loyalists to head public enterprisesVučić and the SNS party deny corruption and seeking to influence the media.Will it still be a student movement, without students?Although they have not been elected, it is the students who have made the promises to the Serbian people and they will come under pressure to follow through on their manifesto.The ordinary Serbian citizens they chose to represent their movement have "been entrusted with transferring part of the struggle we have been waging on the streets for the past year into the institutions", the students say.In his speech on Sunday evening, Vučić told party supporters that the students had destroyed two years of life in Serbia and they would be defeated "faster than they think".

schema.headline: Serbia's student movement: How and why students brought down Vučić

title: Ballon d'Or Feminin: Alexia Putellas wins award for record-equalling third time
description: Spain midfielder Alexia Putellas has won the Ballon d'Or Feminin for a record-equalling third time, keeping the prize in Spanish hands for a sixth con
body: Spain midfielder Alexia Putellas has won the Ballon d'Or Feminin for a record-equalling third time, keeping the prize in Spanish hands for a sixth consecutive year.Putellas, 32, captained Barcelona to Champions League glory as part of a quadruple in 2025-26, before joining Women's Super League (WSL) side London City Lionesses in July.She joins Spain team-mate Aitana Bonmati on three Ballon d'Or Feminin crowns - her former Barcelona colleague won the award in 2023, 2024 and 2025 after Putellas did so in 2021 and 2022.The past six Ballons d'Or have been won by the Spanish pair, with Norway's Ada Hegerberg (2018) and Megan Rapinoe of the United States (2019) the only non-Spaniards to claim the prize.Putellas' latest victory caps a remarkable return to the pinnacle of world football after suffering a career-threatening anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury in 2022."All the boys and girls around the world - if you love football and if you want to play football, play football. It doesn't matter if you're a boy or if you're a girl," Putellas said."Doesn't matter where you come from. Don't listen if someone tells you, you can't do it. Believe in yourself."She collected the most votes from an international panel of journalists across Fifa's top-50 ranked countries, with Barcelona striker Ewa Pajor coming second and Manchester City forward Khadija Shaw third.Meanwhile, England captain Harry Kane won the men's Ballon d'Or, becoming the first English player to do so since Michael Owen in 2001.While Barcelona are always overwhelming favourites to win the three competitions on offer in Spain, Putellas' performances last season showed that she is still among the world's elite.Nicknamed 'La Reina' - meaning the queen - Putellas scored 21 goals and provided 13 assists in all competitions, ranking her third and second respectively among players across Europe's top five leagues.Seven of those goals came in the Women's Champions League as Barcelona claimed a fourth continental title in six seasons.Only Pernille Harder (eight), Alessia Russo (nine) and Ewa Pajor (11) scored more, all of whom are strikers by trade.But Putellas' contributions to Barcelona's attacking play went far beyond scoring goals herself.In Liga F - which Barcelona won for a seventh consecutive season - she finished joint-sixth for assists (seven) and fourth for open-play chances created (40).Across Europe's top five leagues, only Claudia Pina (199), Vicky Lopez (183) and Georgia Stanway (168) recorded more sequence involvements ending in an open-play shot than Putellas (151).In all competitions, she created more chances (89, 19 of which were big chances) and completed more passes ending in the final third (965) than any other player in Liga F, the Champions League, Copa de la Reina and Supercopa de Espana.Only Bayern Munich's Klara Buhl created as many chances as Putellas in the Champions League last season (36), the most by a player in a single edition of the competition since Caroline Graham Hansen in 2021-22 (38).Putellas was born and grew up in the Catalan municipality of Mollet del Valles, about 12 miles north-east of Barcelona.She began playing football in the street, and soon became a Barcelona fan and a regular attendee at Camp Nou.With matches always on the TV at home, former Spain and Barcelona star Andres Iniesta and Brazilian duo Rivaldo and Ronaldinho quickly became her idols.After attending a summer football camp run by Xavi and playing for local side CE Sabadell, Putellas spent a year at La Masia, Barcelona's famous youth academy.Spells at Espanyol and Levante followed the disbandment of her girls team, before she eventually returned to Barca in 2012.Cue the start of a 14-year career with her childhood club during which she won 38 trophies, including 10 league titles and four European cups.But after winning the Ballon d'Or for the first time in 2021, one of the toughest moments of Putellas' career came when she suffered an ACL injury on the eve of Euro 2022, ruling her out of the tournament.Though she retained the Ballon d'Or later that year, it took a while for her to return to her best level. Playing only a bit-part role in Spain's triumphant 2023 World Cup campaign would have stung.After scoring in the 2024 Champions League final and improving further the following season, in 2025-26 she shouldered much of Barcelona's creative burden as Aitana Bonmati missed five months through injury and ended the season a quadruple winner.If that was not enough, the midfielder scored twice in a 4-0 thrashing of England in June that secured Spain's place at the 2027 World Cup at the Lionesses' expense.With her contract at Barcelona expiring and keen for a fresh challenge, Putellas made the decision to leave her childhood club. She, and her fans, were distraught.She had several offers from England, Mexico and the United States, but joined the ambitious project of US billionaire Michelle Kang at London City Lionesses in July."I'm just always looking forward to better things and that's why I'm here too, because I always need to be moving as a person and a player," Putellas told BBC's Women's Football Weekly podcast in August.With three goals and one assist in seven WSL games for her new club, it is clear Putellas is still deserving of her nickname.

schema.headline: Ballon d'Or Feminin: Alexia Putellas wins award for record-equalling third time

title: Backlash after Trump invokes 9/11 in attack on El-Sayed
description: El-Sayed's opponents have sought to link him to the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist organisation that was founded in Egypt. Trump designated certain c
body: El-Sayed's opponents have sought to link him to the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist organisation that was founded in Egypt. Trump designated certain chapters of it as Foreign Terrorist Organisations earlier this year. Some of the scrutiny of the affiliations of El-Sayed and his family members relates to their writings from more than a decade ago. A social media post, external in 2012 by El-Sayed's half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, appeared to refer to the movement, saying "my family has long been MB". El-Sayed's team have previously distanced him from other comments by Abdelhadi.Critics have also pointed to an opinion piece El-Sayed wrote in Huffington Post in 2011, external about pro-democracy protesters in Egypt. In it, he acknowledged concerns that "supporting democracy in Egypt might allow the country to fall to the hands of the Muslim Brotherhood".A year later he also allegedly signed an open letter by Egyptian Americans. In it, the group urged Mohamed Morsi, Egypt's first democratically elected president and a leader of the Muslim Brotherhood, to "purge the media and police" following the toppling of the authoritarian regime in the Arab Spring. This letter has not been discussed by El-Sayed.El-Sayed has previously denied any connection to the Muslim Brotherhood and has stressed his loyalty to the United States. Asked recently at a town hall event whether he would disavow the organisation, he responded: "Absolutely."Also in 2012, El-Sayed's current opponent Rogers, who was then a US representative and chairing the House Intelligence Committee, appeared to call for cautious engagement with the Muslim Brotherhood, telling Reuters, external: "Do I think there are moderate Muslim Brotherhood individuals we are going to have to reach out to and talk to? Yes but we are going to have to watch it carefully." HA Hellyer, senior associate fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) and an expert on Egypt, says the row has more to do with Islamophobia on the political right in the US than with the Trump administration's actual position on the Muslim Brotherhood."If the accusation is to be taken sincerely, then [Trump] should surely have a problem with engaging with any government that has engaged positively with the Brotherhood or with groups that are even more to the right of the Brotherhood," Hellyer told the BBC. "He clearly has not done that." Among the others who condemned Trump's attacks were one of his key supporters ahead of the 2024 presidential election. "The president's statements are out of line," Bishara Bahbah told the Associated Press. "They are crossing a red line. They are racist."Bahbah was the founder of Arab Americans for Trump, a group believed to have been important in helping the president connect with a wider range of voters two years ago. The group later changed its name, removing the reference to Trump. Trump clinched the White House in 2024 after victories in Michigan, which has a prominent population of Arab Americans, and a number of other swing states.Asked about accusations of Islamophobia, White House spokesman Davis Ingle said: "Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed wants to massively raise taxes, advocates for defunding the police, and wants to destroy the Michigan auto industry by banning gasoline powered vehicles. "President Trump will continue to call out complete and total extremists like El-Sayed without apology."Additional reporting by Jake Horton and Tom Bateman

schema.headline: Backlash after Trump invokes 9/11 in attack on El-Sayed

title: Storm Boelo clean-up begins as thousands left without power
description: A clean-up operation is under way in parts of the UK after Storm Boelo caused flooding and property damage, leaving thousands without power.The Energy
body: A clean-up operation is under way in parts of the UK after Storm Boelo caused flooding and property damage, leaving thousands without power.The Energy Networks Association (ENA) said around 22,600 properties were still without power as of Monday afternoon. Two men were killed by falling trees during the storm on Sunday - a man in his 20s whose car was hit in north London and a 60-year-old man in Dumfries and Galloway identified as Richard Baines, the long-serving curator of Logan Botanic Garden.A yellow warning for strong winds came in effect at 18:00 on Monday across the west coast of England, Wales and Scotland and eastern parts of Northern Ireland and will last until 03:00 on Tuesday. The Met Office has warned that further power cuts in areas covered by the warning are likely and people should make sure they have essentials prepared, including torches and batteries.Coastal communities could also be affected by spray or large waves, while travel delays are expected.Boelo is the second storm to have hit parts of the UK in recent days, following Storm Austen.Leo Slade, CEO of the ENA said it had been "a tough weekend" and that efforts to reconnect some properties were being hampered by the weather, with sustained winds of 50-85mph across parts of Scotland and northern England."Until that weather system passes, we can't safely get engineers out to replace poles, to get wires back up, so today is going to be a hive of activity in getting engineers out into the field," Slade told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.He stressed that the UK's power network was very resilient and money was spent to prepare for these sorts of scenarios, but said a debate was needed over how much more investment was required to mitigate for further storms brought by climate change.Marcus Reed, the operations director at a home fragrance manufacturer, said his factory and shop in Lyndal, Cumbria would be without power until Tuesday evening.He told the Today programme that he has had to turn away employees and customers."To lose two days manufacturing and distribution is going to be really disruptive," he said, adding that it was bad timing as it was "the busiest time of the year" for his business in the lead-up to Christmas."This is probably the worst situation I've experienced in my time here; we've had ad hoc issues over weekends where we've lost power, but it's been contained within a 12-hour period. It's the first time anything like this has happened, it's very serious."Wendy McKinney, whose bathroom shop in the seaside town of Largs in North Ayrshire was flooded on Sunday, told the Today programme the storm had been "devastating to local businesses".She said the local council only handed out sandbags after flooding had already started:"[They] were just left in the middle of the street yesterday afternoon on pallets just for everybody just to try and help themselves, but it was too little too late."North Ayrshire Council told the BBC that it had distributed almost 300 sandbags in Largs and Saltcoats and would continue to "respond where it has been safe and appropriate to do so".A spokesperson said council teams "followed established resilience procedures" but would review flooding reports and "consider any lessons that can be learned".

schema.headline: Storm Boelo clean-up begins as thousands left without power

title: Brazil election: How 'Lula's Army' WhatsApp channel helped turn race around
description: The emergence of Lula's Army convinced many supporters that Brazil's left had finally found a way to compete in a digital arena. The shift was particu
body: The emergence of Lula's Army convinced many supporters that Brazil's left had finally found a way to compete in a digital arena. The shift was particularly significant because social media has played a central role in Brazilian politics since Jair Bolsonaro's 2018 election victory, when WhatsApp networks became a defining feature of political campaigning.Lula's Army messages often included ready-made templates for followers to share with friends and family. Each one assigned supporters a specific task aimed at boosting Lula's visibility on social media.Janones frequently instructed his "troops" to "blow up" the latest campaign video or help a new hashtag "take off"."Guys, urgent!", "Don't go to sleep yet", "No food before the mission!", and "I have one more task before you're dismissed", were some of the instructions.On the eve of the election, the congressman also hosted a 24-hour live event - dubbed the "turnaround livestream" - even as polls continued to suggest a victory for Bolsonaro.The tactic worked, despite worries by some members of the Workers' Party that Janones's often-confrontational style on social media could undermine the more moderate image they hoped to project for Lula.In his victory speech, Lula referred to Janones as "our General" and thanked him for "raising the morale of our troops every day".Measuring the electoral impact of online mobilisation, however, is notoriously difficult. While Lula's allies credit Lula's Army with helping fuel the comeback, political scientists caution that it is impossible to determine how many votes, if any, were directly influenced by the WhatsApp operation.Political scientist Denilde Holzhacker argues that a shift in Lula's campaign strategy was key to his comeback. Rather than relying solely on online engagement, she says the Workers' Party candidate succeeded in connecting digital campaigning with grassroots mobilisation on the ground.According to Holzhacker, the campaign intensified local efforts and adapted its messaging - linking a Bolsonaro victory with concerns about potential changes to social programmes and the loss of rights."It was to Lula's credit that he recognised his own weakness and completely changed his style," she says. "And Janones managed to do something that had seemed unthinkable for Brazil's left - dominate social media."By contrast, Holzhacker argues that Flávio Bolsonaro entered the run-off overly confident of victory and failed to communicate his message to his supporters as effectively.Sociologist and political scientist Mayra Goulart, a professor at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, also cautions against attributing Lula's comeback solely to social media."It was a combination of social media and street-level mobilisation," she says. "The physical world enabled a form of mobilisation capable of reducing abstention and persuading undecided voters."In her view, Lula's supporters succeeded in turning online enthusiasm into real-world political engagement."Those committed to Lula's victory worked to bring people together and persuade them to vote," Goulart says.She argues that the effort not only helped increase turnout but could also prove valuable for Lula's next administration."I believe this collective effort was an important learning experience and will prove valuable for a government that still faces many battles ahead. It not only helped reduce abstention, but also converted a significant number of undecided voters."Lula himself suggested that the mobilisation behind his comeback could shape the way he governs in the years ahead.In his victory speech, he said the election had taught him many lessons and pledged to change the way Brazil is governed."We are going to give people a greater say in decision-making, and digital communication will play a much bigger role in my government."

schema.headline: Brazil election: How 'Lula's Army' WhatsApp channel helped turn race around

title: Drivers jailed over deaths of mum and daughter in Leeds
description: Two men who killed a mother and her four-year-old daughter as they raced their high-performance cars along a Leeds city centre road have been jailed.J
body: Two men who killed a mother and her four-year-old daughter as they raced their high-performance cars along a Leeds city centre road have been jailed.Justyna Hulboj, 27, and her daughter Lena Czepczor were killed when they were hit by an Audi TT RS as they walked to the girl's nursery on the A61 Scott Hall Road on 16 January 2023.At Leeds Crown Court on Monday, Hardeep Bhachu, 29, was jailed for 12 years and Jasskamal Riyat, 37, for 16 years.Sentencing the men, Judge Singh said the road was "not a race track" and told them the deaths had consequences that were "immeasurable", with an "immense" impact on those left behind.Bhachu, of Grant Row in Adel, had earlier admitted two counts of causing death by dangerous driving, while Riyat, of Buckstone Avenue in Moortown, was convicted by a jury after denying he had been racing him.The court heard the pair, who did not previously know each other, accelerated away from traffic lights on Scott Hall Road shortly before the crash.Prosecutors said Riyat's BMW reached speeds of up to 89mph in the 40mph zone before Bhachu lost control of his Audi, mounted the pavement and struck Hulboj and her daughter.Susannah Proctor, for Bhachu, told the court that her client was a "normal person who's made a massive mistake".She said he "must live with himself in the knowledge of the devastation he has caused".And she said: "He did not intend to cause this devastation but cause it he has."Hulboj's fiancé Dominik Czepczor watched the sentencing hearing in court.A statement from him was read, which said: "My whole world collapsed in one second."Every day I feel a huge void after their departure."We had so many hopes and dreams and in one moment it all ended."My dream was to have a wonderful family, and I must say that it came true for a short while, but that was taken away from me on January 16."Unfortunately, all that remains are wonderful memories and a constant fight for the next day, which is not easy."Det Insp Paul Conroy, of West Yorkshire Police's Major Collision Enquiry Team, said: "A woman and her young daughter have died because of the actions of these men, and I know no sentence will ever feel enough to compensate for the lives that have been lost."This sentencing hearing though does mark the end of a long criminal justice process for Justyna and Lena's family."It is over two years since Bhachu admitted his part in this tragic incident and I know that the wait for justice has taken its toll."My thoughts are firmly with them today."

schema.headline: Drivers jailed over deaths of mum and daughter in Leeds

title: Five ways Trump has changed immigration in the US
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByBernd Debusmann Jr and Mike HillsImmigration has always been central to Donald Trump's message.When he famously stepped on
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByBernd Debusmann Jr and Mike HillsImmigration has always been central to Donald Trump's message.When he famously stepped onto the golden escalator at Trump Tower to announce his candidacy for his first presidential term in 2015, he accused Mexico of sending drugs and crime north of the border - and it's been a constant rallying cry ever since.Some of his first-term ambitions to stem the flow of would-be immigrants were constrained by the courts.But restraints have been weaker in his second term, with a more accommodating Supreme Court and tens of billions of additional enforcement money from Congress.Who should be allowed to live in the US remains a big issue on the minds of voters in the upcoming midterm elections, which are largely seen as a referendum on the Trump presidency.He promised a closed border and mass deportations in his successful 2024 campaign - and few can deny that he's delivered on both.But even among those who voted for a tougher stance, there is a concern that the crackdown has gone too far.His signature policy has played out in five key ways.1. A border that is largely closedCrossings exploded during Joe Biden's presidency, with over 4.5 million migrant "encounters" recorded at the southern border in 2023 and 2024 alone, reflecting the massive numbers of people headed north to the US border.His administration eventually brought the monthly figures down significantly by restricting asylum claims and removing migrants entering the US illegally without processing.When Trump returned to office, that stream of migrants became a trickle. Border encounters plummeted.By the end of Trump's first year in office, the chaotic scenes that had generated headlines around the globe during the Biden administration had largely gone.On a trip to the border city of El Paso, Texas, in November 2025, for example, the BBC found quiet streets where there had previously been makeshift camps housing thousands of migrants granted parole in the US to await immigration proceedings.To achieve what he often describes as the "most secure" border in US history, the Trump administration has taken an aggressive, multi-pronged approach.That has included effectively freezing asylum applications at the border, ending "catch and release" of detainees into the US, deploying troops to the border and pressuring Mexico to clamp down on the flow of migrants headed north."President Trump promised the American people a secure border, and the data proves he delivered," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement on 16 October."The results could not be clearer: strong enforcement works."2. Building of wall speeding upA vow to build a "big, beautiful wall" at the nearly 2,000-mile (3,218km) US-Mexico border was a signature promise of Trump's 2016 campaign.Progress on it has speeded up in his second term, boosted by $46.5bn (£34.7bn) in new funding from Trump's "One Big Beautiful" spending bill.According to government figures, external, about 644 miles of "primary wall" - closest to the border - existed before Trump returned to the White House, in addition to 75 miles of "secondary" wall set slightly further inside the US.Since then, 250 more miles of new wall have been completed, including primary, secondary and waterborne barriers, along with the technology that helps detect illegal crossings. An additional 1,443 miles of barriers are currently under construction.Experts, however, paint a more complex picture of what has been actually built rather than just improved or updated.Additionally, the impact the wall is itself having on the broader immigration figures is up for debate."Since new wall construction has really begun in earnest, there has been no significant change in the number of people crossing the border," said Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, an immigration enforcement expert at the American Immigration Council.There is no indication the border wall has reduced migrant crossings, he added. The reduction has been more down to Trump's policies and messaging.Trump, for his part, continues to point to the wall as a successful policy - and continues to claim that Mexico paid for it."I'm the King of the Wall," Trump said at a rally in Kentucky on 17 October. "By the way, Mexico did pay for that wall. I charged them tariffs and I charged them costs like they've never paid in history."3. Detentions and deportations rocketingMost of the headlines generated by Trump's immigration policies have come from the US interior, where operations by Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents to round up people they say are in the US illegally have rocked cities across the country.During his campaign, Trump promised an immediate start to what he described as the "largest deportation operation in American history", which officials said would begin with people who have committed crimes first.Arrests - and subsequent detentions in immigration facilities - have shot up significantly since Trump returned to office, including a record of nearly 50,000 in July this year alone, according to data obtained by the Deportation Data Project, external, a repository of US immigration data run out of University of California, Berkeley, and UCLA.But the same data, external shows that a large chunk of the arrests involve people without criminal convictions. In July 2026, detentions of immigrants with criminal histories reached an all-time low of 27%.Deportations have also ramped up significantly. By mid-July this year, ICE was removing an average of 1,255 people from the country per day, compared to about 770 in Biden's final months in office - although Biden's own removals had sharply risen in his final year in office.But the tactics used by ICE in US cities have made many Americans grow uncomfortable, including many of those who supported stricter restrictions broadly. This became increasingly evident following Operation Metro Surge, a two-month large scale enforcement action in Minneapolis in early 2026 that left two US citizens dead.A New York Times and Siena poll, external released on 21 October found that 50% of voters trust Democrats to handle the issue, compared with 46% for Republicans - despite the issue being a traditional Republican strength.A separate poll, from Politico and Public First, external in late September, found deep splits between Republicans on the issue, with 31% of non-MAGA Republicans, meaning those not aligned with Trump's movement, believing that campaign has become too aggressive.Figure caption, Watch: Texas voters share concerns over cost of living ahead of midterms4. Refugee intake down sharplyAfter returning to the White House last year, Trump almost immediately suspended refugee admissions, saying at the time these could only restart if they were shown to be in US interests.In February, however, an executive order signed by Trump narrowly re-opened that process for Afrikaners from South Africa, who the White House has repeatedly said are being killed and "persecuted" - a claim that the government in Pretoria has denied.The cap for refugee admissions for the 2026 fiscal year was initially set at 7,500, which was raised to 17,500 in May this year because of what the administration described as an "unforeseen emergency refugee situation".Overall refugee admissions have slowed to a relative trickle. State Department data shows that 16,292 refugees were admitted into the US in the 2026 fiscal year - of whom 16,287 were South African.By comparison, in the final two fiscal years of the Biden administration - 2023 and 2024 - 60,000 and 100,000 entered the country, respectively. In the 2024 fiscal year, the highest numbers came from Democratic Republic of Congo, Afghanistan, Syria and Venezuela.Hundreds of thousands of people protected from deportation lost that protection when a humanitarian protection called Temporary Protected Status (TPS) was also ended in Trump's second term. It gave vetted individuals the right to live and work in the US if their home countries were deemed to be unsafe to return to.One of those countries was Haiti. In June, the Supreme Court upheld the Trump administration's decision to end TPS for some 350,000 Haitians in the US.5. A squeeze on visas - and a $1m golden ticketOther legal pathways to come to live and work in the US have also been tightened up, through various policy changes.Dozens of countries the Trump administration has deemed a security risk have been subject to a full or partial freeze on visas and travel.Enhanced vetting and new rules that send people residing in the US back to their home countries to apply for green cards has slowed that process down.And in September 2025, a $100,000 fee on new H1-B visas for skilled workers, mostly held by Indians, stunned the US tech industry. In May this year, the US Citizenship and Immigration Services said on X, external that registrations for 2027 were down 40%."The data is a clear sign that the days of abusing the program with mass, low-wage registrations are over, and that the program is better serving its intended purpose of attracting highly skilled foreign workers and protecting the wages, working conditions and job opportunities of American workers," the statement added.While a court has blocked the $100,000 fee - for now - the threat of it appears to have deterred employers. But some experts have cautioned the administration's aim of protecting American jobs, raising wages and stopping firms from outsourcing may prove elusive.One study, from the Wharton School of Business, external, found that the H1-B changes would have "no significant impact" on the wages of US-born workers, with any reduction in competition offset by reduced productivity growth.Other pathways to the US have been opened, however - if you have a spare million.The "Trump Gold Card" launched in 2025 sought to entice wealthy foreigners to come live in the US in exchange for a $1m "gift" to the US government, plus a non-refundable $15,000 application fee.At the time, Trump said that the programme would boost the US economy. Its uptake, however, appears to be minimal so far. By April, only one applicant had been accepted.

schema.headline: Five ways Trump has changed immigration in the US

title: Man Utd: Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann on list if Michael Carrick sacked
description: Michael Carrick has left Manchester United's training ground following talks over his future, with Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann emerging as early
body: Michael Carrick has left Manchester United's training ground following talks over his future, with Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann emerging as early contenders to replace him if he is sacked.Carrick's position at Old Trafford is under major threat following the club's poor start to the season, with work towards identifying his successor believed to be ongoing.It is understood Howe and Nagelsmann both feature prominently on the list of candidates the club has explored to potentially replace him, and that both managers are aware of United's interest.Sources have also indicated Aston Villa boss Unai Emery is admired at United, but the fact he is under contract would complicate any move for the Spaniard.Howe, Nagelsmann and Antonio Conte - who is interested in the job - are out of work, making their potential appointments easier.Multiple sources have told BBC Sport that former Newcastle boss Howe is fully open to joining United if Carrick loses his job.Nagelsmann is available after leaving his job as Germany head coach after the World Cup, while Conte - who has also been linked with Juventus - is open to returning to football after leaving Napoli in May.Carrick left United's Carrington training ground at around 17:00 GMT on Monday.Should he be dismissed, the 20-time English top-flight champions will be looking to appoint their eighth permanent manager or head coach since Sir Alex Ferguson departed the club in 2013 on the back of winning their most recent title.Here, BBC Sport takes a closer look at the contenders who could be up for the job.

schema.headline: Man Utd: Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann on list if Michael Carrick sacked

title: Healey vows cheaper marmalade and gherkins in pre-Budget package
description: Marmalade, for example, will see a 20% tariff, plus an additional £19 charge per 100kg imported, suspended.Healey said the ongoing wars in Iran and Uk
body: Marmalade, for example, will see a 20% tariff, plus an additional £19 charge per 100kg imported, suspended.Healey said the ongoing wars in Iran and Ukraine had "hit families here at home through higher everyday costs". "We can't control global events, but we can act where we can make a difference," he added.Other measures the government announced include:Making permanent a 55p per mile tax-free mileage rate for those driving up to 10,000 miles for work, with the rate rising from 25p per mile to 35p above thatAllowing carers to earn more than an existing earnings limit without losing their entire allowance, replacing it with a taper mechanism insteadGiving two weeks of paternity pay to self-employed fathers, who have previously missed out on payments of up to £194 a week for the periodAnd rolling out hundreds of additional Post Office drop boxes to make sending parcels easierPrime Minister Andy Burnham said: "We are taking on the big challenges facing the country. But that doesn't mean losing sight of the everyday problems that cost people money or simply aren't fair."If you're a nurse driving for work, a parent spending those precious first weeks with your new baby, or an unpaid carer picking up an extra shift, these changes will make life a little easier and put more money back in your pocket."But the Conservatives said Burnham's "everyday fixes" have already been wiped out by higher borrowing costs, taxes and inflation.Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith said: "Shoppers face rising costs at the till and families are struggling to make ends meet, but Burnham's plan is cheaper gherkins. This is an insult to families hammered by Labour's tax rises."

schema.headline: Healey vows cheaper marmalade and gherkins in pre-Budget package

title: Busted's James Bourne says 'hero' brother saved his life with kidney donation
description: Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, James Bourne: "I can't believe how much better I'm starting to feel already."ByIan YoungsCulture reporte
body: Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, James Bourne: "I can't believe how much better I'm starting to feel already."ByIan YoungsCulture reporterBusted star James Bourne has said his brother "saved my life" by donating a kidney, after doctors had given him "a few years left to live".The guitarist, 43, dropped out of an arena tour featuring his band and fellow punk-pop favourites McFly in September 2025, just a day before it began.He blamed health problems and was replaced by his younger brother Chris.James later said he needed major surgery to "extend my life", and has now thanked his "hero" Chris and said they are both recovering from their transplant operations.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Bourne with his Busted bandmates Charlie Simpson and Matt Willis in 2023"Wow, what the hell happened?" James wrote on Monday. "One minute you're heading out on tour, the next thing you know you're on the bench and out of the game."My condition was serious and the doctors told me I had a few years left to live."I'm happy to share now that my youngest brother, Chris, who stepped in for me on tour last year, has saved my life yet again. This time quite literally by donating me one of his kidneys."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Chris Bourne went on tour with Busted after his brother was forced to drop outJames continued: "I can't believe how much better I'm starting to feel already."I'm still going to need some time, but I wanted you to know that we're both recovering from surgery just fine. My brother is a hero."Chris posted his own message on X saying simply: "We did it brother."Bourne has not given any more details of his condition.Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, Busted had eight top 10 hits in the UK between 2002 and 2004The guitarist, vocalist and songwriter shot to fame with Charlie Simpson and Matt Willis in Busted in the early 2000s, and the trio had hits including What I Go To School For, Year 3000 and Crashed the Wedding.They scored four number one singles in the UK before splitting up in 2005. In 2013, Bourne and Willis teamed up with McFly to make McBusted, before Simpson rejoined Busted for a full reunion in 2015.Bourne has written songs for McFly and 5 Seconds of Summer, and also fronted his own band, Son of Dork. He recently released the music from his stage musical Murder at the Gates.

schema.headline: Busted's James Bourne says 'hero' brother saved his life with kidney donation
